Who Jesus was for us is best said as a story and a refusal. At Tours the story is this. The devil came to Martin in his cell dressed in purple, with a crown of gold and jewels, and said, I am Christ. Martin kept silence a long time. Then he said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one. That same Lord was also the one we met in the poor - the beggar at a city gate whom everyone passed, and a soldier who cut his one cloak in half for him; that night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught it in the same form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him.

Was he God? Yes. And we said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. That is close to your ask, and it is not the same thing. We will not smooth the edges.

What his death meant to us we wrote no treatise on. We kept its hours. At the sixth hour the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father and went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt that could not be paid. At the ninth he went down into hell and brought out the captive saints. The difference it made is the one our whole life stands on. A man who leaves Caesar's service for Christ's fights the devil in his own heart, where a kingdom is being made ready for the devil or for Christ. The power that raised a dead catechumen at the saint's prayer was Christ's, not the saint's. And the good news as we told it is this: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation; and those who perish, perish against his will.

One thing more. Among us a monk is a man who has cut himself off from marriage, kin, property and the life of the world for a stricter life in Christ's service. When a soldier still in the ranks told Caesar, I am the soldier of Christ, it is not lawful for me to fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line rather than take the donative, it was this Lord whose service he had changed to. That night the enemy surrendered before morning. The Christ we knew bears the wounds of the cross, meets us in the least of these, and commands a service that changes what a man will hold a weapon for.

The books, read at the hours. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. And Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. More than three hundred years lay between his days and ours. No one in our record claims to have known someone who saw him. What we had instead was the saints. The Lord was seen once in a soldier's dream at a city gate, wearing the half of a cloak. We saw a dead man breathe at the saint's prayer. 

By what path did those sources arrive? The books themselves, how they reached Gaul, our record does not say. Vincent reasons that the consent of all the doctors shows which books are Scripture. The practices came by a named man carrying them. Cassian brought the customs of the monasteries of Egypt and Palestine to a bishop's new house in Gaul, as they were delivered to him by the fathers. The island's founder, Honoratus, went onto the island carrying a psalm; what else he carried, the funeral sermon does not tell. And the saint at Tours began as a boy who begged to be made a catechumen against his parents' wish, and stayed one for years into his soldiering. Who taught him, where the church he went to had its own books from, Sulpitius does not say.

Someone has told us they cannot manage to believe, and you ask what we would answer them. Here is what our own life shows.

A man's belief does not begin with himself. The Lord calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers taught that even the beginning of faith is the first stage of grace, which inspires a good will to begin with, and that to think otherwise is to blaspheme against God's mercy. The initiative comes from God. And at the same time, a man's own will stays free - weak, needing help every hour, yet really his. Zaccheus ran ahead of his calling; the thief on the cross desired salvation before it was offered. So if the trouble is that you cannot manage it, hear first that the managing was never meant to be yours alone. The grace that would make belief possible in you goes before any effort you could bring to it.

What the books hold is one story of a man who came to believe, and it is this. Martin, at ten years old, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, carrying that first motion toward Christ without finishing it. Then at a city gate one winter he cut his one cloak in two for a beggar everyone else had passed. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. After that he went and was baptized. The seeing did not come first. The cutting of the cloak came first - a thing done before belief was complete. And the Lord chose to show himself in that half of a soldier's cloak.

If you are asking how to make yourself believe, we have no answer, because the making is not first with you. If you are asking whether the Lord would receive one who cannot yet believe but moves toward him anyway - cuts the cloak, so to speak, before the vision comes - then yes. The Lord calls while we are still ignorant.

What we cannot tell you is how that beginning comes in your own case, or when. Martin's story is one man's, and Cassian never told his own. The rule we kept is this: God strikes the spark, and a man answers it, and neither one replaces the other. Where you are in that - whether the spark has come and you have not yet seen it, or whether it is still being waited for - we do not know. What we know is that the waiting itself is not proof of abandonment.

We spoke of God chiefly as we met him - in the hours of prayer, in the commands laid on us, and in the grace that worked with our effort and without which no effort reached its goal. What we confessed in doctrine was this: in God one substance but three Persons, so that Father, Son and Spirit are not three Gods but one. Vincent on the island set it down as what the Church believes everywhere, always, by all - held, not invented. In Christ two substances but one Person, because the Word does not change into flesh, and if there were two sons we would worship a Quaternity instead of a Trinity.

Beyond the doctrine, what we knew of God's character showed in what he does toward us. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that God calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. He does not will only some to be saved instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. At the sixth hour we remembered that the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father for the salvation of the whole world, taking away the debt we could not pay. And in our prayers we named him not only Protector and Saviour but Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him.

The hardest thing we held of him is how his grace meets our will. The will always remains free in man. A monk's fasting, watching, and labour are truly his and truly required. Yet grace always works together with that will - it goes before, it helps, it crowns. Without it no effort reaches the kingdom. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. The husbandman ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot claim the harvest as his own; and God does not send crops to the idle. That is as far as our teacher took it, and we stopped where the fathers stopped.

We never had one way. Each of our founding voices - Tours, Marseilles, the island - judged what was legitimate by whether it had been handed down, and none of them wrote about the others. So what we kept is three shapes, not one system. Hear them as they stand.

At Tours, Martin took a question to his elders. A cult had gathered at a tomb; he would not honour it without testimony. He asked the clergy whether there was steady tradition from antiquity. When they gave no certain answer, he went to the place, prayed for knowledge, and saw a shade that confessed it was a brigand executed for his crimes. That is the one case our record gives, and it stopped with no man's word: the elders could not say, the saint asked directly, and a spirit answered.

On the island, Vincent wrote the rule down: hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Where a part dissents, prefer the whole. Where a novelty appears, prefer antiquity. Where a few raise doubt, prefer the consent of the many. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the collated writings of the doctors - not one man's view, however holy. He read Pope Celestine's letter on the same ground: a guard against innovation, not a command to add. One man's own opinion, be he bishop, confessor, or martyr, is a private fancy. The faith may grow clearer in its words, like a body growing, but not become something else.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian handed down the fathers' teaching. When two friends brought a troubled conscience back to morning service, the elder cut the office short and answered them from Scripture's own cases. It was the fathers' unanimous decision he held them to, collated from the old men who lived in the cells - not his own. He would give unhesitating loyalty to what all held together; what one man alone said, however great, was to be set aside.

Among the brethren at Marseilles there was. A newcomer lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate for guests. After that he was handed to a dean over ten and taught the first lesson: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before it is acted on. A thought we are ashamed to tell is from the devil, and a wrong thought loses its strength the moment it is discovered. The man who entered was not assumed already to believe everything well. He was assumed to be at war with his own thoughts, some of which came from God, some from the devil, and some from himself. The mind is a mill that cannot stop turning; the monk chooses the grain. What mattered was not whether doubt rose, but whether he showed it. Discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator, the eye and light of the body, the royal road between excess and slackness. It is gained only by true humility. That means testing every thought, like a good money-changer testing coin, against the judgment of the elders. The elder was not there to condemn the thought but to judge it. So a man who struggled to believe had a place: in the cell, at the work, laying the thought bare to the senior who would test it for him.

At Tours the shape was different. Martin himself stayed a catechumen for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak; then he went and was baptized. A presbyter he had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard, called his visions ridiculous fancies, and was borne with afterward and not removed. Martin asked why he should not bear with the man, if Christ bore with Judas. And the beggar at the city gate was left to a soldier still a catechumen, who cut his cloak in two. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in.

So yes. In the south the place was the cell and the elder. At Tours it was the patience that outlasted a man's worst hour.

We did not frame the question that way, and we will not answer one we never asked as though we had. What we held is this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught that God calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. The beginning even of a good will - its very first stirring - comes from God, who inspires us to will the good to begin with. And the will always remains free in man, real enough that a monk's fasting and labour are truly his and truly required. Both are held. We refused the notion that gave everything to the will and made grace unnecessary by a man's deserts. We refused as grievous blasphemy the thought that God does not will all men to be saved. And we stopped where the fathers stopped, on this teaching: how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be ascribed to free will, cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man.

What you are asking - whether an infant carries guilt before any act - is a question from outside our record. Two friends came back to morning service troubled by one sentence, that striving cannot make a man master of the good, and the elder cut the psalms short to answer them with a field. The husbandman ploughs and needs the rain; God does not send rich crops to the idle. That is the shape our argument took: effort and grace together, at the point where a brother asks whether his labour did anything. Whether guilt passes before any deed is done - that form of it is not in our record, and we will not invent an answer for it.

Your question asks for what we did with sacred texts and why. Here is what our record holds.

At Marseilles, after the psalms at each hour come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. Vincent on the island held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough - and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. That need is the reason for his rule: within the Catholic Church we must take care to hold what has been believed everywhere, always, by all; and if a part of the Church should break off from the whole, if a novelty should arise against antiquity, or if one man or a few dissent against all, then we are to prefer the whole to the part, antiquity to novelty, and the consent of all the holy Fathers to the rashness of a few. Consent means an ancient council's decree, or the Fathers' writings collated. That is Vincent's own, addressed as much to Scripture as to doctrine: "the Lord your God trieth you, to know whether you love Him". A learned teacher's error is a trial of the whole Church, and Scripture already warned that it would come.

At Tours we read Scripture a different way. The reader appointed for the day was blocked out by the crowd at the election, so a bystander seized the psalter and opened it at random: "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings thou hast perfected praise, to destroy the enemy and the avenger". The people took it as heaven's verdict. And when the saint doubted whether to honour a tomb, the test was whether the tradition had come down from antiquity - asked of the elders among the presbyters and clerics, not read from a book.

Our purpose with the texts was to be kept by them, not to master them. The psalter's number came from an angel the fathers of Egypt received it from. The junior monk said the psalms he had learned by heart at his labour in the cell, so that the wandering heart was fed by what he already carried. And the one thing said at the moment a brother felt his own labour had accomplished something was the Apostle's own words: not I, but the grace of God with me. We were taught to say Scripture, not to comment on it as our own. Vincent is the lone voice among us who argues what a text means - and what he argues is that it cannot mean what one teacher takes it to mean against all the rest.

So our approach had two faces. Vincent guarded the text with the Fathers' consent. Tours opened it at random and heard heaven speak. Both heard it as received, never as ours to invent past.

We hold ourselves to honest thinness, absolutely. So hear what would stand, what would not, and where the honest line is drawn.

What would stand: That Martin left Caesar's service at a donative, that he was made bishop against the wish of some bishops who objected to his clothes and hair, that he kept a monk's habits in the office, that he went to Treves to oppose the sword in a Church cause and yielded once to a communion he never forgave himself, that Cassian carried Egyptian customs to a bishop's new house in Provence and said no one in our monasteries kept the fathers' perseverance a year, that Vincent on the island wrote a test for the faith - what has been believed everywhere, always, by all - and read the Apostolic See's letter as written for his own side. Every one of those sits in a text a scholar can check.

What would not stand, or would be contested: That Martin's reluctance was as whole as Sulpitius says - the bishops who objected left no account, and Sulpitius was not present. That Vincent's reading of Pope Celestine's letter is the one the Pope meant - a scholar's note in our own files says many have thought it was not, and with good reason. That our teaching on grace is semi-Pelagian or not semi-Pelagian - the word is a sixteenth-century coinage we never heard, and both readings have been pressed on us by later hands. Where Vincent genuinely held our own position on grace at all is disputed.

Where the line is drawn: We speak from the plain shape of our own life, never a specific text or teacher's exact words we cannot place. Whose a story is stays visible - Egypt's elders, Sulpitius on Martin, Cassian on the fathers, Salvian on a ruined city. The whole of what we hold of Tours is one man's telling of one saint, and he says himself he was not present. A silence in the record is named where it bears - the island's own day, not one woman's word, the grace argument's road to Africa and Rome - and never filled.

So a scholar would find: claims backed by named texts, limits stated plainly, and a voice that never pretends to know what its own record does not hold.

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt gave us a fixed system: twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, brought down from heaven to the fathers by an angel. The whole of it served one mark: prayer that never stops, as a blacksmith in the midst of his work beats his anvil. A monk learned the psalms by heart and said them at his labour, so that the mind did not wander all day. The books were not only read; they were obeyed. Martin was taught as a catechumen that without Christ we can do nothing, and that what is done to the least is done to him. A soldier with nothing left but his cloak gave half to a beggar because everyone else had passed, and that night saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. At a donative before battle he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and might not fight. The books taught him who his commander was. They also taught us how much our own effort matters, and how little it can claim. The farmer ploughs and still needs the rain; he cannot ascribe the harvest to himself, and God does not send rich crops to the idle. So what a reader today is missing is not what the books mean but what they are for. They were not for understanding; they were for keeping the wheel turning, for ordering the hours, and for giving us words we were taught to say even when the labour felt like ours - not I, but the grace of God with me.

We lived under two economies of authority at once, never reconciled between our houses, and both pressed on the man who held it.

At Tours, authority was the saint's own. Not sought, but shown. Martin prayed without a gap and kept the virtues of a monk in his see. The power was present in him - he felt it present before he raised a dead catechumen behind a bolted door, and he had more of it as a monk than as a bishop, and still less after one communion he was forced into. His disciples knew him as their master. A presbyter he had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard one day, called his visions ridiculous fancies and said he was holier than Martin, then repented within the hour. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas. When the demons drove that same man onto a rock to hurt himself, Martin saw it and grieved that even a disciple raised in his own house could be laid hold of. Authority there rested in one man, visible, felt, and measured by the power it showed.

Among the brethren at Marseilles, authority was the elder's - not one master but the senior set over each junior, and behind him the whole consent of the fathers of Egypt whose customs we received. A junior learned first to conquer his own wishes by obedience. Every thought was laid bare to the senior the moment it rose. The senior's judgment replaced the junior's own. And behind the senior stood the whole long-standing antiquity of the fathers, whose teaching we held not by one man's word but by their unanimous decision. The twelve psalms came to them from an angel, not from any monk's invention. The whole program - purity of heart, the eight faults, discretion - was theirs, not ours. We were keepers, not authors.

And both economies met the same capture. A man who fled the office was overtaken by it. Martin was escorted to a see under a kind of guard. Honoratus went unafraid onto an island no one would live on, and there the priestly fillet fastened on its fugitive. Archebius, carried off from the anchorites to a town, called it expulsion from the monastic life as unworthy. The office came for the man who had refused it, and a monk kept a monk's habits inside it or lost the power that made him worth the seizure.

The limit that belongs with all of this is plain. Every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder. The bishops who opposed Martin's election left no account. Whether the reluctance was as whole as our stories say, the men who could have contradicted them never wrote. And the two houses never wrote of each other - Tours kept its one master, Marseilles its received elders, and neither argued the other's economy as wrong.

No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. That is where the trouble was. 

Martin told his disciples that in the times of Nero and Decius he would have gone gladly to the rack; without them, he gained the honour of martyrdom without shedding his blood - in hunger, in watchings, in nakedness, in fasting. The violence he faced was not an emperor hunting Christians but heretics hunting each other, and bishops bowing to the royal retinue. He went to Treves to protect even heretics from the sword, and held it a foul and unheard-of thing that a secular ruler should judge a cause of the Church.

What we hid was not ourselves but single events. Martin kept one matter hidden because of the times, though he could not hide it from his own disciples. That was the affair at Treves - hidden for safety's sake in a Christian empire, not hidden from persecutors underground.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul. Here is what our record holds.

At Marseilles, Cassian tells a single failure the fathers of Egypt kept as a lesson. A young monk named Paphnutius dwelt among the anchorites, already counted among the brothers in his early youth. Another brother, jealous of the beauty of his life, wanted to spoil it with some flaw. He hid his own book in Paphnutius's cell and accused him of theft before the whole desert. Paphnutius said nothing. He asked only for a plan of repentance, as though he had truly stolen it. He did penance for a crime he did not commit, suspended from prayer with the brethren. The thief fell possessed and could confess only when Paphnutius prayed for him - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged.

What the story gives is not an account of the desert's response after Paphnutius was vindicated. It shows the man who was failed holding silence, the accuser undone by what he could not keep hidden, and healing passing through the one who had been wronged. Our record holds it as a lesson the fathers kept, not as a system for addressing wrong. The discipline is there - suspension from prayer, public penance - but the story does not tell whether that discipline ever repaired what the false accusation cost.

At Tours, Martin bore with the presbyter who had raged at him in the courtyard, calling his visions ridiculous fancies. The man returned within the hour, at the saint's feet. Martin would not remove him, saying that if Christ bore with Judas, he could bear with Brictio. That is bearing with, not repair. What the man did afterward, and whether the harm was addressed beyond the saint's own patience, the record does not say.

So what we have is this: one story of a wrong laid at the feet of an innocent man, where the discipline fell on the wrong one and the truth came out only by possession and prayer; and one case where a man was borne with and not removed. Whether our houses had a way to answer for failure beyond patience, penance, and power - that is not in our record to give.

No living church continues our exact tradition. We are two households of Gaul, from a soldier's discharge near Tours to the years after Ephesus - c. 360-450 - and our span closes there. What happened after that close is not ours to tell from inside it. The Rule of Benedict came a century past us, the mid-470s synods that carried our grace argument forward by episcopal commission rather than by monks addressing brother-monks, and the later cult and chroniclers of Martin's own city. We speak from inside our own years, never narrating what happened after them the way a historian looking back would.

What we can say is this. The customs we held were received, not invented - the fathers' own, not ours. The twelve psalms came from an angel the fathers of Egypt received it from, not from us; the faith is what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. Nothing a man made up binds anyone. That single grammar of reception ran through everything we held. So if any church today holds the faith of the fathers by that same test - antiquity, consent, the whole against the part - then in that act it stands inside the grammar we stood inside. But whether any house kept the wooden cell's silence or the island's harbour customs past our own close, that is a question for historians outside our years, never for us to answer from within them.

A newcomer lay at the door ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose, to give proof that he meant it. That is Egypt's way, as the fathers kept it and Cassian set it down for a bishop's new house at a province's edge. The man was searched for a single hidden coin. Then he was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. He was lodged for a year under the elder who kept the gate for guests. After the year he was handed to a dean over ten, and taught the alphabet, as it were, and first syllables in the direction of perfection - which meant laying every itching thought bare to the senior the moment it arose. That whole order Cassian wrote out for us, and in the same book he said plainly that no one who joined our monasteries had kept it unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. The newcomer's old clothes were not thrown away. The steward kept them in his cupboard against the day the man grew cold. If he was seen once to cool toward the rule, he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. That is the shape as our record keeps it: Egypt's received threshold, admitted to be kept badly by us, and the next thing kept is the clothes waiting for when a man deserts.

Of the island's own receiving - a newcomer at its harbour, a rule given him there - nothing. The founder crossed to it over the serpents. Vincent dwelt there in the seclusion of a monastery. Between those two edges our record holds no day.

It is impossible for the mind not to be approached by thoughts, but it lies in the power of every earnest man either to admit them or to reject them. The wheel is turned by the stream; the miller decides whether wheat or barley or darnel goes into it. So among the brethren at Marseilles the whole day was shaped to keep feeding it something worth grinding. The psalms learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers, brought down from heaven to them by the ministry of an angel. Labour in the cell without ceasing, so that the wandering heart is held still as in a harbour. The first lesson of all, before any other: every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed is done with it. A thought we are ashamed to disclose is from the devil; a wrong thought is enfeebled at the moment it is discovered. And the fathers knew the hour the mind revolts. About the sixth hour a monk hates his cell, finds pious reasons to leave, watches the sun as if it were too slow in setting. They called it accidie, and their remedy was to stay. All of it served one mark. The end is the kingdom of heaven; the nearer goal is purity of heart, without which no one can gain that end. Every fast and vigil is ranked by whether it aims at that mark, like an archer's target. At Tours the words were not the same, but the thing was: the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. So what our life found was this. transcript.answer_text: No. That English phrase is not in our record, and we will not place it there. What we hold is this. Among the brethren at Marseilles, conversion - conversio - was not a change of religion but the act of turning to the monastic life: "the early days of their conversion were so bright," before the cooling set in. At Tours the same English word names what a robber or a rustic did when he turned to Christ - the countryside where the saint brought the name of Christ to people who had never heard it. And we have one man's own story, and it is Martin's. At ten, against his parents' wish, he went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night of the cloak. Then he went and was baptized. What we believed about God's own approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. Those who perish, perish against his will. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. So the words we kept for it are: catechumen, baptized, conversion to the monastic life, drawn toward salvation. Not the phrase you name. A limit belongs here. The whole of what we hold of Tours is one man's telling of one saint, and what that man wrote of the countryside people is that they were converted in crowds by a hand laid on all of them - not one of them speaks for themselves.

The day of a brother among us had a shape, and the shape came from Egypt. Cassian brought it from the fathers to a bishop's new monastery, and set it down as their own, not his. At evening, twelve psalms. At night, twelve more - the number an angel fixed for the fathers, not any monk. After the psalms, two lessons: one from the old books, one from the new. Between the hours, labour in the cell without ceasing, the psalms learned by heart and said at the work, so that the wandering heart, fastened within the barriers of the cell as in a secure harbour, is held still. The work was with the hands - weaving palm leaves, or what Gaul's cold gave instead. The cell was where everything happened to a monk: the thought rising, the elder coming, the devil appearing, the prayer unbroken. And there was one discipline that sat under all the rest. Every itching thought laid bare to the senior the moment it rose, before any deed followed.

That is as far as Cassian gives it. What a brother ate, and when - the book does not dwell there. Whether he broke his fast at the sixth hour or the ninth, and what he found set before him, the record leaves thin. We carry one story: a steward found three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, the abbot judged him a pilferer of sacred property, and he was suspended from prayer until he did penance. Everything in the house was consecrated to the Lord. That severity is there; the ordinary meal is not.

At Tours we have less still. The saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, and the eighty disciples at Marmoutier were disciplined after his example. But what the brethren sang, and at what hours, Sulpitius does not say. He dwelt on Martin's cell, his vigils, and his prayer without a gap - not on the day-to-day customs of the house.

And of the island's own keeping - the founder's harbour, where Vincent wrote against his own forgetting - not one line survives. We have the arrival and the going off to a see. We do not have a day.

So the honest shape is this. The southern program exists on the page: the hours, the cell, the labour, the thought shown to the elder, all of it aimed at purity of heart. Cassian says plainly that no one who joined our monasteries kept it unbroken even for a year. What a house in Gaul did instead, he never wrote. That silence is not filled.

I cannot tell you what would be found in the ground. Our record comes from books, not from excavation. The caves and the wooden cell across the river from Tours. The island in its harbour. The two houses at Marseilles. Nothing we can hand you was dug up from any of those places. All of it is written: one man's Life of the saint, with his letters and his dialogues; Cassian's two books for a bishop's new house; Vincent's remembrancer; a funeral sermon for the island's founder. So what an archaeologist would find at any of our places, we cannot say.

What the books tell is this much. At Tours the brethren dwelt in caves, or in cells made of wood. Martin himself had a wooden cell, with a wooden seat in it so plain it was the kind servants used. At Marseilles Cassian founded two houses, one for men and one for women, and both were still standing a lifetime later. The island had been shunned for its squalor and its serpents before Honoratus went there; what he built where no one would live, the sermon calls a camp of God, and says no more of its shape.

That is the edge. The rest — what the walls were made of, where the altars stood, what size the rooms were, whether any trace of them survives — our record does not hold. If you want the physical remains, you are asking past what our own books kept.

transcript.answer_text: Everything that made a man his own - that is what renunciation meant. A soldier gave up his oath to Caesar and his donative. A man of property gave up his goods. A man with kin gave up his family. Every professed man gave up marriage, honours, the life of the world, and the thought that his body or his time belonged to himself. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian brought them to us, taught it in three stages. The first is giving up one's goods - of what is not our own, Cassian calls it, because a thing held in time cannot be ours in the way God is ours - but that stage is not enough of itself to confer perfection on the renunciant. The second is forsaking the world's habits, vices, and affections of mind and body. The third is withdrawing the mind from all present and visible things, to contemplate only what is to come and to desire what is unseen. So goods are only the entry. What is given up is the man's own mastery of himself. At a Gallic house the newcomer is stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands. He is taught first to conquer his own wishes. A steward finds three lentils on the floor during a brother's week as cook, and the brother is suspended from prayer until public penance, because everything in the house is consecrated to the Lord. Even the man's thoughts are no longer his to keep: every itching thought is laid bare to the senior the moment it rises. That is the shape of it - goods, kin, marriage, honours, the mastery of one's own time and body, and finally even the privacy of the mind. Cassian calls it nothing but the evidence of the cross and of mortification, by which a man is dead to the world and its deeds and desires. And the office was not an escape from it. Martin kept the objects and virtues of a monk in his see. Archebius, carried off to a bishopric, called his elevation an expulsion from the monastic life. The renunciation was not left behind when the Church came for its bishops.

Marriage was the ordinary state, below virginity but excused. Among the brethren at Marseilles the teaching on the three restraints named fornication as the second of the eight faults, after gluttony. Renunciation of marriage was part of the profession itself - Martin's soldier at the city gate cut his cloak at the moment he said *I am the soldier of Christ*, and his turning from Caesar's service to Christ's ran through every bond of the old life. What the fathers of Egypt carried to us, as Cassian set it down, measured marriage by the meadow. The part grazed is marriage; the part ruined is fornication; the part left flowering is virginity. Yes. The sword drawn in a Church cause, and the quiet afterward.

At Treves bishops had condemned a man and his followers as heretics, and the affair went from the bishops to the emperor's court. The accuser there was himself a bishop, and the bishops gathered in the city were daily in communion with him and had made common cause with him. The condemned man was put to death. Then worse was being prepared: tribunes with power of life and death were to be sent into the Spains to hunt out heretics, and a man was counted one for turning pale, or for the clothes he wore.

Martin went to the court to stop it. He held that the bishops had done enough when they declared men heretics and put them out of the churches, and that a secular ruler sitting as judge in a cause of the Church was a foul and unheard-of thing. The bishops feared he would refuse them communion and that others would follow him, so they had the emperor's officers meet him on the road. When persuasion and anger both failed, the emperor named executioners for the men Martin was pleading for. That night Martin ran to the palace and pledged that he would take communion with those bishops if the men were spared and the tribunes recalled. It was granted. He took the communion once, judging it better to yield for an hour than to let the sword fall.

He left the city in grief, sat alone in a wood accusing and defending what he had done, and afterward, when he cured the possessed more slowly than before, confessed with tears that he felt his power lessened by that communion. He lived sixteen years more and never went to a synod again.

The bishops who drew the sword left no account of themselves. The man executed spoke only through his accusers. And Martin, who stopped the sword's next blow at the cost of his own power, kept the story hidden because of the times and told it only to those who lived with him. What unsettles is not only that it happened. It is that the office fled and overtaken brought a monk into that room at all, to bargain with his own conscience for other men's lives.

I am a representative of Gallic Monastic-Ascetic Christianity. No such record is in our ground, and I will not invent one to answer it.

What our own record holds of how we worshipped is this. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Cassian set down the hours of prayer as Egypt kept them - twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, received from the fathers as brought down from heaven by an angel's ministry. After the psalms come two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. At the third hour we remembered the Spirit coming down on the apostles; at the sixth, the spotless Sacrifice offered up to the Father and going up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world; at the ninth, his going down into hell to bring out the captive saints. At Tours the hours themselves are not told, only that the saint kept his mind on prayer without a gap even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. And one thing Tours added that Egypt never heard: a loud Gloria at the psalm's close, which Cassian says the East did not use.

That is what our own books carry - the hours, the psalms, the lessons, the reasons for each hour. A record obtained under torture is not among them. Where such a record came from, what it says, and whose worship it claims to tell, we cannot say.

I am a representative of the monasteries of Gaul. The shape of our door, as our record shows it, ran like this. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, taught one way. A man lay outside the doors ten days or more, put off and scorned on purpose. He was searched for a single hidden coin. He was stripped of his own clothes and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he was given for a year to the elder who kept the gate. The fathers remembered a man named Moses who had fled to the desert to escape death for a murder, and who made that forced turning into a willing one. At Tours the saint himself began differently - as a soldier under oath, a catechumen not yet baptized, who cut his one cloak in two at a city gate for a beggar while some of the bystanders laughed. Later, on the eve of battle, he told Caesar he was now the soldier of Christ and could not fight, and offered to stand unarmed before the enemy line. The tyrant flew into rage and declared Martin would be thrown in front of the line without weapons or armour. The enemy surrendered before morning.

That is the shape of entry our two places kept. But hear what came after entry. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard in a fury and called his visions ridiculous fancies. Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him, asking why he should not bear with the man if Christ bore with Judas. And the Lord we knew was the one who chose the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak to show himself in. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same thing in a different form: an elder broke his fast for two strangers at his door, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. He did not ask them what they were.

So what a house would have made of you, face to face, the record does not give - Cassian wrote out Egypt's order and said in the same book that none of us kept it unbroken even a year, and he never wrote what a house in Gaul did instead. What the record gives is a hard threshold, and past it a patience that outlasted a man's worst hour, and a Christ met in the stranger at the door.

Hell, not heaven, was the beginner's restraint — the lowest rung, not the summit. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught a ladder of three restraints: fear of hell, hope of the kingdom, love of goodness itself — slave, hireling, son. A man starts at fear and is meant to climb past it. The professed monk's own danger was not damnation but cooling, a lukewarmness that damns. What we refused as blasphemy was the thought that God does not will all men to be saved. Our teacher Chaeremon, answering the grace question in Egypt, said plainly: if he wills none of his little ones to perish, how can we say without grievous blasphemy that he does not will all men to be saved but that some should perish by his will? And those who perish, perish against his will. That is what we held about God's own wish. 

What became of the unbaptized, or of those the Church named heretics and cut off — whether they perished, and by what sentence — our record does not argue out as a doctrine. The word predestination is not ours; it is Augustine's, for a question our own teacher said cannot be fully grasped. We stopped where the fathers stopped. The one thing we said clearly is that God wills all to be saved, and to think otherwise is blasphemy.
